insert.title: How BTreeMap::insert works
insert.description: Like HashMap::insert, but the keys are always kept in sorted order.

slides.caption: A BTreeMap keeps its keys sorted, so iterating always gives them in order.
Choose BTreeMap when you need sorted keys or ranges; HashMap is usually faster for plain lookups.

range.title: How BTreeMap::range works
range.description: Iterates over the entries whose keys fall in a range, in order.

slides.caption: Because the keys are sorted, range can jump straight to the first key >= 2.
7 is past the end (5 is excluded): the iteration stops.
Great for time ranges, scores between two values, or "everything after this key".

first_key_value.title: How BTreeMap::first_key_value works
first_key_value.description: The entry with the smallest key.

slides.caption: The keys are sorted, so the smallest one is always at the start.
last_key_value() would give (9, "z"). An empty map gives None.
pop_first() also removes it, which makes a BTreeMap usable as a priority queue.

btreeset-insert.title: How BTreeSet::insert works
btreeset-insert.description: A set that keeps its values sorted.

slides.caption: Each value is placed in sorted position; a value that is already there is ignored.
1 is already in the set: insert returns false and nothing changes.
A quick way to get the unique values of a list in sorted order: v.into_iter().collect::<BTreeSet<_>>().

push_front.title: How VecDeque::push_front works
push_front.description: Adds an item at the front, without shifting the others.

slides.caption: A VecDeque is a ring buffer: it can grow at the front as cheaply as at the back.
2 and 3 stay where they are in memory.
1 is written in front of them, without moving anything.
Vec::insert(0, x) would move every item. Use VecDeque when you add or remove at the front often.

pop_front.title: How VecDeque::pop_front works
pop_front.description: Removes the first item: a queue, first in, first out.

slides.caption: Items are added at the back with push_back and taken from the front with pop_front.
1 was added first, so it leaves first.
2 is now at the front, ready to be next.
push_back + pop_front is a queue (first in, first out); push_back + pop_back is a stack.

push_back.title: How VecDeque::push_back works
push_back.description: Adds an item at the back.

slides.caption: push_back appends at the end of the queue.
Together with pop_front, this is the standard way to build a queue (for example for breadth-first search).

push.title: How BinaryHeap::push works
push.description: Adds a value; the largest value is always on top.

slides.caption: A BinaryHeap is not sorted, but it always knows its largest value.
3 is pushed: it is the largest so far.
8 is pushed and rises to the top.
peek() shows the top without removing it. Wrap values in std::cmp::Reverse to get the smallest on top instead.

pop.title: How BinaryHeap::pop works
pop.description: Removes and returns the largest value.

slides.caption: Each pop takes the current largest value off the top; the next largest takes its place.
Then 3. One more pop would give None.
Popping everything gives the values from largest to smallest. Priority queues and Dijkstra's algorithm are built on this.
pop_back takes the item at the back of the deque.
3 is at the back: taken out.
A VecDeque can be used from both ends, as a queue or as a stack.

peek.title: How BinaryHeap::peek works
peek.description: Shows the largest value without removing it.

slides.caption: The largest value is always at the top of the heap, so peek is instant.
Nothing is removed: the heap still has 3 values.

get.title: How BTreeMap::get works
get.description: Looks a key up in a sorted map.

slides.caption: get walks down the tree, comparing the key, until it finds it or knows it is missing.
5 is not in the map: None.
Lookups take about log₂(n) comparisons, still fast for large maps.

pop_first.title: How BTreeMap::pop_first works
pop_first.description: Removes and returns the entry with the smallest key.

slides.caption: The keys are sorted, so the smallest key is the first entry.
1 is the smallest key: (1, "wake") is removed and returned.
Keys as priorities: a BTreeMap works as a simple ordered work queue.

last_key_value.title: How BTreeMap::last_key_value works
last_key_value.description: The entry with the largest key.

slides.caption: The largest key is always at the end of a BTreeMap.

entry.title: How BTreeMap::entry works
entry.description: The same entry API as HashMap, with sorted keys.

slides.caption: Counting with a BTreeMap gives the result already sorted by key.
Pick BTreeMap when you want the counts printed in order.

split_off.title: How BTreeMap::split_off works
split_off.description: Moves every entry with key >= k into a new map.

slides.caption: split_off(&3) cuts the sorted map at key 3.
3 and above move to the new map.
append(&mut other) is the opposite: it merges two maps.

btreeset-range.title: How BTreeSet::range works
btreeset-range.description: The values inside a range, in order.

slides.caption: Because the set is sorted, range jumps to 5 and walks until 11.
Great for questions like "which scores are between 50 and 80?".
A BTreeSet is sorted, so its smallest and largest values are at the ends.

front.title: How VecDeque::front works
front.description: The first item, without removing it.

slides.caption: front and back just look; nothing is removed.
Both return None for an empty deque.

rotate_left.title: How VecDeque::rotate_left works
rotate_left.description: Moves the first n items to the back.

slides.caption: rotate_left(1) is like a round-robin: the first item goes to the end of the line.
Cheap on a VecDeque: no items are copied around in memory.

make_contiguous.title: How VecDeque::make_contiguous works
make_contiguous.description: Arranges the ring buffer as one slice, so it can be sorted.

note.text: a deque has no sort of its own

slides.caption: A VecDeque may wrap around inside its buffer. make_contiguous puts it in one piece and returns a &mut slice.
The items are moved into one continuous run.
The slice can now be sorted.
as_slices() lets you look at the two halves without moving anything.

into_sorted_vec.title: How BinaryHeap::into_sorted_vec works
into_sorted_vec.description: Consumes the heap and returns its values sorted, smallest first.

slides.caption: The heap repeatedly takes its largest value and places it at the end: that is heap sort.
Ascending order, even though pop() gives largest first.

len.title: How BinaryHeap::len works
len.description: How many values the heap holds.

note.text: push adds one, pop removes one

slides.caption: len counts all values, not just the top.
while let Some(x) = h.pop() empties it one by one.

new.title: How BTreeMap::new works
new.description: An empty map that keeps its keys sorted.

slides.caption: Whatever the insertion order, iteration goes from the smallest key up.
Pick BTreeMap when you need ordered output or range queries; HashMap is usually faster otherwise.

remove.title: How BTreeMap::remove works
remove.description: Removes a key and returns its value.

slides.caption: Removing a missing key returns None and changes nothing.

contains_key.title: How BTreeMap::contains_key works
contains_key.description: true if the key is in the map.

slides.caption: A lookup in a sorted tree: about log₂(n) comparisons.
Use get when you also need the value.
keys() walks the tree from smallest to largest.
Sorted keys for free: a big reason to choose a BTreeMap.

values.title: How BTreeMap::values works
values.description: The values, in the order of their keys.

slides.caption: Values follow the sorted keys, not insertion order.
Iteration is always ascending by key.
iter().rev() goes from the largest key down.
len is stored, so it costs nothing to ask.

is_empty.title: How BTreeMap::is_empty works
is_empty.description: true if the map has no entries.

get_mut.title: How BTreeMap::get_mut works
get_mut.description: A mutable reference to the value for a key.

slides.caption: get_mut returns None if the key is missing.

first_entry.title: How BTreeMap::first_entry works
first_entry.description: The entry with the smallest key, to read, change or remove.

slides.caption: first_entry gives an OccupiedEntry for the smallest key.
Its entry is removed; "a" is returned.
pop_first does exactly this in one call.

last_entry.title: How BTreeMap::last_entry works
last_entry.description: The entry with the largest key.

slides.caption: Change the value of the largest key in place.
Returns None for an empty map.

pop_last.title: How BTreeMap::pop_last works
pop_last.description: Removes and returns the entry with the largest key.

slides.caption: Repeated pop_last processes keys from largest to smallest.

retain.title: How BTreeMap::retain works
retain.description: Keeps only the entries that pass a test.

slides.caption: The closure sees each key and value; false removes the entry.
The order of the remaining keys is unchanged.

append.title: How BTreeMap::append works
append.description: Moves every entry of another map into this one.

slides.caption: On equal keys, the value from b wins.
Key 2 is moved over; b is now empty.
Faster than a loop of inserts when the maps are large.

range_mut.title: How BTreeMap::range_mut works
range_mut.description: Mutable access to the values whose keys lie in a range.

slides.caption: Only the keys from 2 to 3 are visited.

values_mut.title: How BTreeMap::values_mut works
values_mut.description: Mutable references to every value, in key order.

into_keys.title: How BTreeMap::into_keys works
into_keys.description: Consumes the map and yields its keys in order.

into_values.title: How BTreeMap::into_values works
into_values.description: Consumes the map and yields its values in key order.

slides.caption: The keys are dropped; order follows the keys.
All keys and values are dropped.

btreeset-new.title: How BTreeSet::new works
btreeset-new.description: An empty set that keeps its values sorted.

title.text: let mut s = BTreeSet::new(); for x in [5, 1, 3, 1] { s.insert(x); }

slides.caption: Duplicates are ignored and the order is always ascending.
Sorted unique values with one call: v.into_iter().collect::<BTreeSet<_>>().

contains.title: How BTreeSet::contains works
contains.description: true if the value is in the set.

slides.caption: A tree search: fast even for large sets.
HashSet::contains is usually faster but unordered.

btreeset-remove.title: How BTreeSet::remove works
btreeset-remove.description: Removes a value; true if it was there.

slides.caption: Removing a missing value returns false.
take() returns the removed value itself.
Iteration always goes from smallest to largest.
The tree is walked in order.
iter().rev() goes from largest to smallest.
The duplicate 1 is stored only once.

btreeset-is_empty.title: How BTreeSet::is_empty works
btreeset-is_empty.description: true if the set has no values.

slides.caption: Typical loop: while let Some(x) = s.pop_first() { ... }.
In a sorted set, the maximum is at the end.

btreeset-pop_first.title: How BTreeSet::pop_first works
btreeset-pop_first.description: Removes and returns the smallest value.

slides.caption: A BTreeSet can act as a sorted work queue without duplicates.

btreeset-pop_last.title: How BTreeSet::pop_last works
btreeset-pop_last.description: Removes and returns the largest value.

slides.caption: Repeated pop_last visits values from largest to smallest.
Returns None when the set is empty.

union.title: How BTreeSet::union works
union.description: Every value in either set, in sorted order.

slides.caption: Values in both sets appear once.
1 and 3 from a, 2 from b; 3 only once.
&a | &b builds the union as a new BTreeSet.

intersection.title: How BTreeSet::intersection works
intersection.description: The values that are in both sets.

difference.title: How BTreeSet::difference works
difference.description: The values in this set that are not in the other.

slides.caption: Everything from a, minus what b has.
2 is in b, so it is left out.
Not symmetric: b.difference(&a) would be empty here.

symmetric_difference.title: How BTreeSet::symmetric_difference works
symmetric_difference.description: The values in exactly one of the two sets.

slides.caption: Shared values are dropped; the rest stay.

is_subset.title: How BTreeSet::is_subset works
is_subset.description: true if every value of this set is also in the other.

btreeset-append.title: How BTreeSet::append works
btreeset-append.description: Moves every value of another set into this one.

slides.caption: 1 is already in a; 2 moves over.
extend() copies instead, leaving the source untouched.

btreeset-retain.title: How BTreeSet::retain works
btreeset-retain.description: Keeps only the values that pass a test.

slides.caption: Values for which the closure returns false are removed.

btreeset-split_off.title: How BTreeSet::split_off works
btreeset-split_off.description: Splits the set: values ≥ the given one move to a new set.

slides.caption: Everything from 5 upwards goes into the returned set.
BTreeMap::split_off works the same with keys.

vecdeque-new.title: How VecDeque::new works
vecdeque-new.description: An empty double-ended queue: fast to add and remove at both ends.

title.text: let mut q = VecDeque::new(); q.push_back(1); q.push_front(0);

slides.caption: Unlike Vec, inserting at the front is cheap.
The standard queue for breadth-first search and job lists.

with_capacity.title: How VecDeque::with_capacity works
with_capacity.description: An empty deque with room for n elements.

slides.caption: Avoids growing while the queue fills up.

back.title: How VecDeque::back works
back.description: The last element, without removing it.

slides.caption: front() looks at the other end.
len is stored, so asking is free.

vecdeque-is_empty.title: How VecDeque::is_empty works
vecdeque-is_empty.description: true if the deque has no elements.

slides.caption: while let Some(x) = q.pop_front() is often neater.

vecdeque-get.title: How VecDeque::get works
vecdeque-get.description: The element at an index (0 = front), or None.

slides.caption: Indexes count from the front, wherever it is in memory.
q[1] also works but panics when out of range.

vecdeque-get_mut.title: How VecDeque::get_mut works
vecdeque-get_mut.description: A mutable reference to the element at an index.

slides.caption: Returns None if the index is out of range.
front_mut and back_mut cover the ends.

vecdeque-iter.title: How VecDeque::iter works
vecdeque-iter.description: Visits the elements from front to back.

slides.caption: Even if the buffer wraps around in memory, iter goes in queue order.
iter().rev() goes from back to front.

vecdeque-insert.title: How VecDeque::insert works
vecdeque-insert.description: Inserts an element at an index, shifting the shorter side.

slides.caption: VecDeque moves whichever side has fewer elements.
Insertions in the middle are still O(n); the ends are O(1).

vecdeque-remove.title: How VecDeque::remove works
vecdeque-remove.description: Removes and returns the element at an index.

slides.caption: Returns None for an index that does not exist.
swap_remove_back is faster when order does not matter.
Reuse the same queue in loops.

vecdeque-contains.title: How VecDeque::contains works
vecdeque-contains.description: true if an equal element is in the deque.

slides.caption: contains checks each element in turn.
For frequent lookups, keep a HashSet beside the queue.

drain.title: How VecDeque::drain works
drain.description: Removes a range of elements and yields them.

slides.caption: Take the first n jobs in one step.

truncate.title: How VecDeque::truncate works
truncate.description: Keeps only the first n elements.

slides.caption: Elements beyond the first n are dropped.
Panics if an index is out of range.

vecdeque-range.title: How VecDeque::range works
vecdeque-range.description: An iterator over a range of positions.

slides.caption: Like slicing, but works even if the buffer wraps around.

as_slices.title: How VecDeque::as_slices works
as_slices.description: The contents as two slices, because the buffer may wrap around.

slides.caption: After push_front, the front element can sit at the end of the buffer.
The first slice holds the front part.
make_contiguous turns it into one slice.

rotate_right.title: How VecDeque::rotate_right works
rotate_right.description: Moves the last n elements to the front.

slides.caption: The deque spins; nothing is lost.

vecdeque-retain.title: How VecDeque::retain works
vecdeque-retain.description: Keeps only the elements that pass a test.

slides.caption: The remaining elements keep their order.
retain_mut lets the closure change elements too.

vecdeque-split_off.title: How VecDeque::split_off works
vecdeque-split_off.description: Splits the deque in two at an index.

slides.caption: Everything from the index onwards moves to a new deque.

vecdeque-append.title: How VecDeque::append works
vecdeque-append.description: Moves all elements of another deque onto the back.

slides.caption: 3 moves to the back of a.

resize.title: How VecDeque::resize works
resize.description: Grows (filling with a value) or shrinks to a length.

slides.caption: New elements are clones of the given value.
Two 0s are added at the back.

front_mut.title: How VecDeque::front_mut works
front_mut.description: A mutable reference to the first element.

slides.caption: Returns None for an empty deque.

back_mut.title: How VecDeque::back_mut works
back_mut.description: A mutable reference to the last element.

slides.caption: Returns None for an empty deque.
Handy for updating the newest entry in a history.

binary_search.title: How VecDeque::binary_search works
binary_search.description: Searches a sorted deque: Ok(index) or Err(where it would go).

slides.caption: Halves the search range each step.
The middle checks narrow it down.
Searching for 4 gives Err(2): insert it at index 2 to stay sorted.

binaryheap-new.title: How BinaryHeap::new works
binaryheap-new.description: An empty priority queue: pop always gives the largest element.

title.text: let mut h = BinaryHeap::new(); h.push(3); h.push(9); h.push(1);

slides.caption: Elements are kept partly ordered so the maximum is always on top.
Wrap values in Reverse(x) for a min-heap.

from.title: How BinaryHeap::from works
from.description: Turns a Vec or an array into a heap in linear time.

slides.caption: Building from a whole Vec is faster than pushing one by one.
The items are rearranged into a heap.
into_sorted_vec then gives them in ascending order.

into_vec.title: How BinaryHeap::into_vec works
into_vec.description: Gives the elements back as a Vec, in heap order (not sorted).

slides.caption: The first element is the maximum; the rest are in internal order.
Use into_sorted_vec if you need sorted output.

binaryheap-drain.title: How BinaryHeap::drain works
binaryheap-drain.description: Removes every element, in no particular order.

slides.caption: drain does not pop in priority order.
For priority order, loop with pop().

peek_mut.title: How BinaryHeap::peek_mut works
peek_mut.description: Changes the top element; the heap reorders when you are done.

slides.caption: When the guard drops, the changed element sinks to its place.
The heap reorders: 5 is the new top.

binaryheap-iter.title: How BinaryHeap::iter works
binaryheap-iter.description: Visits all elements, in arbitrary order.

slides.caption: iter is fine for sums, counts or searches.
Do not rely on the order: it is internal heap order.

binaryheap-is_empty.title: How BinaryHeap::is_empty works
binaryheap-is_empty.description: true if the heap has no elements.

slides.caption: Typical loop condition for processing a priority queue.
while let Some(x) = h.pop() avoids the separate check.

binaryheap-append.title: How BinaryHeap::append works
binaryheap-append.description: Moves every element of another heap into this one.

slides.caption: Merging is efficient: it rebuilds when that is faster.

binaryheap-retain.title: How BinaryHeap::retain works
binaryheap-retain.description: Keeps only the elements that pass a test.

slides.caption: The heap is rebuilt from what remains.
Same as drain() without looking at the elements.

linkedlist-push_back.title: How LinkedList::push_back works
linkedlist-push_back.description: Adds an element at the end of a doubly linked list.

slides.caption: Each element is its own heap node with links to its neighbours.
VecDeque is almost always faster; LinkedList is rarely the right choice.

linkedlist-push_front.title: How LinkedList::push_front works
linkedlist-push_front.description: Adds an element at the front.

slides.caption: The new node becomes the head.

linkedlist-pop_front.title: How LinkedList::pop_front works
linkedlist-pop_front.description: Removes and returns the first element.

slides.caption: The second node becomes the new head.

linkedlist-pop_back.title: How LinkedList::pop_back works
linkedlist-pop_back.description: Removes and returns the last element.

slides.caption: The previous node becomes the new tail.
Returns None for an empty list.

linkedlist-front.title: How LinkedList::front works
linkedlist-front.description: The first element, without removing it.

linkedlist-append.title: How LinkedList::append works
linkedlist-append.description: Moves all nodes of another list to the end, in constant time.

slides.caption: Only two links change, however long the lists are: the one thing linked lists do best.
a's tail is linked to b's head.
split_off goes the other way (but has to walk to the index).

linkedlist-len.title: How LinkedList::len works
linkedlist-len.description: The number of elements (stored, so it costs nothing).

slides.caption: The list keeps a counter; it does not walk the nodes.

linkedlist-contains.title: How LinkedList::contains works
linkedlist-contains.description: true if an equal element is in the list.

slides.caption: contains visits nodes one by one.
Linear time, and slower than on a Vec because nodes are scattered in memory.
